# Individual differences that come from the model

Individual differences estimated by a model, such as the variance of a
random slope, are often read as differences between the people. They can
also come from the model or from how the data are arranged. This article
shows a case where people who are all the same appear to differ in how
fast they change.

``` r

library(ctsem)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Data

Two hundred people are each observed twice, one year apart, starting at
ages between 0 and 3. Everyone follows the same course, rising from 0 at
age 0 towards 5, quickly at first and then more slowly. The measurements
have a little error:

``` r

set.seed(1)
n <- 200
startage <- runif(n, 0, 3)
dat <- data.frame(id = rep(1:n, each = 2), occasion = rep(0:1, n))
dat$age <- startage[dat$id] + dat$occasion
dat$y <- 5 * (1 - exp(-dat$age)) + rnorm(nrow(dat), 0, 0.1)
```

Plotted by occasion, as a two-wave study often is, people seem to
differ: some change a lot between the two occasions and some hardly at
all, and those who start lower change more.

``` r

ggplot(dat[dat$id <= 30, ], aes(occasion, y, group = id)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line() + theme_bw()
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Plotted by age, they all lie on one curve:

``` r

ggplot(dat[dat$id <= 30, ], aes(age, y, group = id)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line() + theme_bw()
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## Two models

A linear growth model on the occasions has a starting level and a slope
for each person. The measurement error is fixed to its true standard
deviation, which two occasions per person cannot separate from the rest:

``` r

datocc <- data.frame(id = dat$id, time = dat$occasion, y = dat$y)
mlinear <- ctModel(type = 'ct',
  manifestNames = 'y', latentNames = 'eta',
  LAMBDA = 1, DRIFT = 0, DIFFUSION = 0, CINT = 'slope',
  MANIFESTMEANS = 0, MANIFESTVAR = 0.1)
flinear <- ctFit(datocc, mlinear, cores = 2)
summary(flinear)$popsd
#>          mean    sd  2.5%   50% 97.5%  mode
#> T0m_eta 1.143 0.061 1.023 1.142 1.263 1.138
#> slope   0.729 0.040 0.649 0.728 0.809 0.726
summary(flinear)$rawpopcorr
#>                  mean    sd 2.5%    50%  97.5%   mode        z
#> slope__T0m_eta -0.998 0.002   -1 -0.999 -0.992 -0.999 -502.866
```

The slopes differ a lot between people, and they are almost perfectly
negatively correlated with the starting levels: where a person starts
predicts how fast they change.

A model on age, with time running from age 0 for everyone, describes the
shape of the course instead. Its process has an auto effect, which slows
the growth as the level rises. Each person gets a row at age 0 with
nothing observed, so that the starting value refers to age 0 for
everyone. The starting value and the intercept still vary over people:

``` r

datage <- data.frame(id = dat$id, time = dat$age, y = dat$y)
start <- data.frame(id = 1:n, time = 0, y = NA)
datage <- rbind(start, datage)
datage <- datage[order(datage$id, datage$time), ]
mdynamic <- ctModel(type = 'ct',
  manifestNames = 'y', latentNames = 'eta',
  LAMBDA = 1, CINT = 'cint', MANIFESTMEANS = 0, MANIFESTVAR = 0.1)
fdynamic <- ctFit(datage, mdynamic, cores = 2)
summary(fdynamic)$popmeans
#>             mean    sd   2.5%    50%  97.5%   mode
#> T0m_eta   -0.011 0.034 -0.077 -0.012  0.059 -0.011
#> drift_eta -1.001 0.013 -1.027 -1.000 -0.977 -1.001
#> diff_eta   0.040    NA     NA     NA     NA  0.031
#> cint       5.007 0.051  4.905  5.004  5.107  5.006
summary(fdynamic)$popsd
#>          mean sd 2.5% 50% 97.5%  mode
#> T0m_eta 0.024 NA   NA  NA    NA 0.024
#> cint    0.001 NA   NA  NA    NA 0.001
```

The auto effect and intercept are close to the -1 and 5 of the process,
and almost no differences between people remain. Both models fit the
same observations, so their log likelihoods can be compared:

``` r

c(linear = logLik(flinear), dynamic = logLik(fdynamic))
#>    linear   dynamic 
#> -156.9604  338.7110
```

The differences between people in the first model came from fitting a
straight line to a curve, with each person observed on a different part
of it.

## What follows

An estimated random effect means the model needs it, which can be
because the people differ, or because the model leaves something out
that varies between them. Here that was age. The same happens when
cohorts of different ages are pooled, or when the time scale of a study
(occasions, weeks since enrolment) is not the one the process follows. A
model with a time scale and a form of change closer to the process
leaves less to explain by differences between people.
